claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.
Helm packages Kubernetes applications as charts, which are directories of templated YAML manifests, a values.yaml file of default inputs, and metadata.
The helm CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax.
The helm CLI either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi supports authoring infrastructure using general-purpose languages with loops, conditionals, classes, and package management, plus YAML and HCL.
Helm charts are authored as YAML manifests with Go template syntax and a values.yaml file for inputs.
Pulumi's resource ordering is derived from the dependency graph, where each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm's resource ordering is fixed by Kubernetes kind.
Helm chart authors can't declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Pulumi's Automation API is a programmatic SDK available in every supported language for embedding up, preview, and destroy in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only, and other languages must shell out to the helm CLI.
Pulumi Policies are open source, with rules in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego.
Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management on top of Pulumi Policies.
The Pulumi Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine, and policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
Helm doesn't let a chart author declare that one resource depends on another.

The Helm docs state that when Helm installs or upgrades a release, the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set, then sorted by type followed by name, and then created/updated in that order.

Helm's installation order is a hardcoded list of Kubernetes kinds in the Helm source, beginning with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list, including custom resources, last.
Helm's uninstall process runs the same kind-ordering list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.
Helm chart dependencies don't change Helm's fixed kind-based ordering.
A Helm subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else.
A Helm chart can't express that the database subchart should install before the application subchart, or that a Deployment should start after a Job completes.

The workarounds for Helm ordering are chart hooks ordered with helm.sh/hook-weight annotations, whose resources Helm doesn't manage as part of the release, or sequencing logic built into the application itself, such as init containers that poll for a dependency.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
Pulumi orders operations from the program's actual dependencies.
Passing one resource's output into another, or setting the dependsOn resource option, creates an edge in the Pulumi dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi deletes follow the same dependency graph in reverse.
The helm.v4.Chart resource supports the config.kubernetes.io/depends-on annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart.
The helm.v4.Chart resource supports the dependsOn option on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Helm manages Kubernetes resources only.
A Helm chart can install Custom Resource Definitions, workloads, services, and other manifests into a cluster.

Pulumi manages non-Kubernetes resources and Kubernetes resources in one program through the Pulumi Registry, which covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms like Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare.
Helm runs as the helm CLI against a cluster and records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision.
The helm rollback command restores a prior release revision.
Pulumi runs through the local CLI, programmatically through the Automation API, or remotely through Pulumi Deployments.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and you roll forward by reverting program code and running pulumi up.

Pulumi handles cluster provisioning and any non-Kubernetes resources, then installs Helm charts inside the same program, either upstream charts from the broader Helm ecosystem or charts authored in-house.

A single Pulumi program can create the cluster (EKS, AKS, or GKE), configure networking and IAM, and install the operational stack, for example cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns, through helm.v4.Chart or helm.v3.Release.

Resource outputs from elsewhere in a Pulumi program, such as a database connection string from aws.rds.Instance, a KMS key ARN, a managed Redis endpoint, or a Cloudflare zone ID, flow into a chart's values input as typed Pulumi outputs.
Pulumi resolves the values at deploy time and orders the chart install after its dependencies.
Choosing Pulumi lets you manage infrastructure beyond Kubernetes, such as cloud accounts, networking, databases, and SaaS platforms, with one tool.
Pulumi supports resources created and deleted in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.
The Automation API is an embeddable SDK that can drive deployments from a host application, such as an internal developer platform, a SaaS product, or ephemeral preview environments per pull request.
You can use Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program with helm.v4.Chart or helm.v3.Release, and migrate incrementally.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program is the most common adoption pattern.
You can convert charts to native Pulumi code by rendering them with helm template and converting the YAML with pulumi convert --from kubernetes.
You can import existing in-cluster resources with pulumi import or the import resource option, which generate the corresponding code.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through helm.v4.Chart and helm.v3.Release.
A Pulumi program can pull charts from any Helm repository, public or private.
A Pulumi program can pass values as typed Pulumi inputs, including outputs from other Pulumi resources, and manage chart lifecycle alongside other infrastructure.

helm.v4.Chart renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
helm.v3.Release uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving Helm-specific behaviors like chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.
Helm chart dependencies cannot control the order resources are installed in.

Helm merges the objects from a chart and all of its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
Ordering within a Helm release requires chart hooks with hook weights or logic in the application itself.
Pulumi can install Helm charts directly through helm.v4.Chart and helm.v3.Release, so teams that want to keep using upstream charts can do so from inside a Pulumi program.
Teams that want to move off Helm entirely can convert charts to native Pulumi code.
The chart's values input accepts the same shape as a values.yaml file but lets each leaf be a Pulumi output.
Pulumi resolves the values at deploy time and installs the chart after the resources it depends on.

You can install existing Helm charts from a Pulumi program and migrate incrementally, convert rendered charts to native Pulumi code with pulumi convert --from kubernetes, or import already-provisioned in-cluster resources.
